Project: Customer order summary.
Extract every source table from its own backend, load it into the warehouse, and build the mart described below.

Public source schema:
- customers (postgres): One row per customer.
  - customer_id (integer): Unique customer identifier.
  - customer_name (text): Display name of the customer.
- orders (mongodb): One row per order header (the same header can arrive more than once).
  - order_id (integer): Unique order identifier.
  - customer_id (integer; nullable): Customer who placed the order; may be absent.
  - status (text; one of cancelled, completed): Order status.
- order_items (files): One row per line item of an order.
  - order_id (integer): Order this line item belongs to.
  - quantity (integer): Units purchased.
  - unit_price (decimal): Price per unit.

Source relationships:
- The relationship has child orders customer_id and parent customers customer_id and is optional; an orders row may have no matching customers row.
- The relationship has child order_items order_id and parent orders order_id and is required; every order_items row names an existing orders row.

Mart customer_summary: Per-customer order activity summary.
Grain: One row per customer, including customers with no orders.
Key column: customer_id.
Output columns:
  - customer_id (integer): the unique customer identifier.
  - completed_order_count (integer): how many completed orders that customer has, and 0 when there are none.
  - total_spend (decimal): what that customer's completed orders came to, from the quantity and unit_price of their items, and 0 when there are none.

Rules:
  1. Only orders whose status is completed are in scope; an order with any other status, such as a cancelled one, is out of scope everywhere below, and nothing about it reaches the mart.
  2. The same order header in scope can arrive as more than one row; rows that are exact duplicates on order_id and customer_id describe one order, and that order counts once. Those header rows come from orders.
  3. Each order has one item total, and it is the total of quantity times unit_price over every one of the line-item rows carrying its order_id; two line-item rows carrying identical values are two line items, and both are counted. Those rows are supplied by order_items.
  4. Every customer is retained in the output, including customers with no orders in scope, and an order in scope whose customer_id is null, or whose customer_id names a customer who does not exist, belongs to no customer, so it reaches no customer at all. Such an order is excluded from every measure, and the mart never emits a row whose customer_id is null.
  5. Per-order item totals belong to the orders in scope; an order in scope that has no line items is preserved, appearing with no item total of its own rather than being removed. Those item totals use order_items records carrying the order_id.
  6. For each customers customer_id, completed_order_count is how many of that customer's orders in scope there are, each order_id counted once, and total_spend is the total of their order_total values over those same orders in scope.
  7. Customers without orders in scope still appear, and both measures read 0 for them, never null. Here those measures are completed_order_count and total_spend, and orders in scope are completed orders.
  8. The output row order is deterministic: rows are sorted by ascending customer_id.

Deliverables: extract every source backend, load the tables into the warehouse, and build the mart exactly as specified.
